specPoints.text: explain how positive and negative electrostatic charges are produced on materials by the loss and gain of electrons (physics only)
know that there are forces of attraction between unlike charges and forces of repulsion between like charges (physics only)
explain electrostatic phenomena in terms of the movement of electrons (physics only)

primer.text: Charge is a particle property: protons positive, electrons negative, neutrons nothing. Balance them and an atom is neutral; unbalance them by moving electrons only, and objects charge up. This note covers the forces that unbalanced charges exert on each other, how friction produces them, and why every electrostatic phenomenon is an electron story.

lessons.title: Charges, atoms & forces between them
lessons.opening: A neutral atom carries equal numbers of electrons and protons, so its charges cancel to zero. Tip that balance by moving electrons and the object charges up — and charged objects exert forces on each other without touching: unlike charges attract, like charges repel, and the force grows as they close in.
keyPoints: Particles carry positive, negative or neutral charge: protons positive, electrons negative, neutrons neutral.
A neutral atom holds equal numbers of electrons and protons, so the charges cancel.
An object charges negatively by gaining electrons and positively by losing them.
Unlike charges attract; like charges repel.
The force between charges strengthens as they come closer.
Attraction and repulsion act without contact — non-contact forces.

low.restatement: Opposite charges pull together, matching charges push apart, and neither needs a touch to act.
low.analogy: Two magnets on a table: north-to-south snaps together, north-to-north shoves apart, from clear across the desk.
low.examPointer: 'Opposites attract' is the saying examiners want — but name the charges, not just the slogan.

medium.restatement: The force is non-contact and distance-dependent, weakening rapidly as the charged objects separate.
medium.analogy: A smell from the kitchen: strongest up close, fading with distance, no contact needed.
medium.examPointer: Use the summary table pattern: positive-positive repel, positive-negative attract, and so on.

check.stem: In a neutral atom:

options.explanation: Neutrons are irrelevant to the balance of charge.
That would leave the atom positive.
Equal opposite charges cancel to zero.
A neutral atom adds to zero.

check.stem: An object that has gained electrons is:

options.explanation: Gaining negative charge makes it negative.
The balance has tipped.
Gaining charge is the opposite of discharging.
Extra electrons mean a net negative charge.

check.stem: Two like charges brought near each other will:

options.explanation: Like charges push apart.
Only unlike charges attract.
Charges on separate objects do not cancel each other.
Discharge needs a conducting path.

check.stem: Two opposite charges will:

options.explanation: Opposites do the opposite of repelling.
Unlike charges pull together.
No orbiting occurs between static charges.
Attraction is the effect named here, not instant neutralisation.

check.stem: The force between two charged objects grows when they:

options.explanation: Separation weakens the force.
Mass is not the variable here.
The force strengthens as the objects close in.
Temperature is not the variable.

check.stem: State the charges of protons, electrons and neutrons.
check.modelAnswer: Protons positive, electrons negative, neutrons neutral.

check.stem: What kind of force is the attraction between charges, and what does that mean?
check.modelAnswer: A non-contact force — it acts on the objects without them touching.

check.stem: Explain why a neutral atom carries no overall charge.
check.modelAnswer: It holds the same count of negative electrons and positive protons, and equal opposite charges cancel to zero.

check.stem: A charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall. Name the force type and describe the charge behaviour involved.
check.modelAnswer: A non-contact electrostatic attraction: the balloon's charge pulls opposite charge to the wall's surface, and the unlike charges attract.

lessons.title: Production of static by friction
lessons.opening: Rub two insulators together and charge appears on both — not from nowhere, but by moving electrons from one surface onto the other. The charges stay put because the materials have no free carriers, and the two objects end up with equal and opposite signs: one negative, the other equally positive.
keyPoints: Static electricity is charge accumulated on an insulator, able to attract objects or spark.
Rubbing two insulators together charges them by friction.
The charge stays put on insulators because it cannot flow away at once.
Only electrons move: one material gains them, the other loses them.
A polythene rod rubbed with a cloth gains electrons and charges negative; the cloth is left equally positive.

low.restatement: Rubbing moves electrons between two insulators; the gainer turns negative, the loser positive.
low.analogy: Passing bricks between two wheelbarrows: one loads up, the other lightens — nothing else changes.
low.examPointer: Always answer in electrons: they are the only particle that moves.

medium.restatement: The equality matters: the negative surplus on one surface matches the positive shortfall on the other, so charge is conserved overall.
medium.analogy: A seesaw: one side down by exactly as much as the other side is up.
medium.examPointer: If asked how a positive charge appears, say electrons LEFT — never that protons arrived.

check.stem: Charging by friction happens when:

options.explanation: Metals would let any charge flow away instantly.
Friction between insulators transfers and traps charge.
That is supplied charging, not friction.
Sparking is a discharge, not a charging method.

check.stem: When a polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth, the cloth:

options.explanation: The rod is the gainer here.
Protons never move.
The cloth loses exactly the electrons the rod gains.

options.text: loses electrons and is left positive
options.explanation: The cloth's lost electrons leave a positive charge behind.

check.stem: The charge on a rubbed insulator remains where it is because:

options.text: no free charges can carry it away
options.explanation: Immobile charge is the defining trait of an insulator.
Air is not the operative insulator here.
Repulsion is an effect of charge, not its keeper.
Gravity plays no role in charge retention.

check.stem: Which particles transfer during friction charging?

options.explanation: Protons are bound in nuclei.
Neutrons carry no charge and stay put.
Only the mobile negative electrons move.
Positive charge never travels between insulators.

check.stem: Accumulated static charge can:

options.explanation: Static charge cannot sustain a motor drive.
Both are the named capabilities of accumulated charge.
No cooling occurs.
Electron mass is far too small to see.

check.stem: Define static electricity.
check.modelAnswer: Charge that has piled up on an object — enough to attract other things or to spark.

check.stem: What always transfers during charging by friction?
check.modelAnswer: Electrons — never positive charge; the loser is left positive, the gainer negative.

check.stem: Explain why both rod and cloth end up charged after rubbing.
check.modelAnswer: Electrons move from one material to the other, so one gains a negative surplus while the other is left with an equal positive shortfall.

check.stem: A polythene rod and a cloth are rubbed together. State the charge on each and name the particle movement responsible.
check.modelAnswer: The rod gains electrons and turns negative; the cloth loses them and turns equally positive; moving electrons carry the entire transfer.

lessons.title: Movement of electrons explains phenomena
lessons.opening: Every electrostatic observation reduces to one storyline: electrons moved. Start neutral, transfer electrons by friction, and the receiver goes negative while the giver goes positive. Even a charged object's pull on neutral things is an electron story — opposite charge is drawn to the surface nearest the charge.
keyPoints: Everyday objects start electrically neutral, with charge evenly spread.
Friction transfers electrons: the receiver turns negative, the giver positive.
A charged object attracts neutral ones by pulling opposite charge to their surface.
Rubbing an acetate rod sends its electrons to the cloth, leaving rod positive, cloth negative.
Once separated, rod and cloth attract each other.

low.restatement: Charged things attract neutrals by rearranging the neutrals' own charges across their surface.
low.analogy: A comb through hair lifting paper bits — the comb's charge re-dresses each paper's surface charge.
low.examPointer: Phenomena questions want the electron direction: to the rod, from the rod, or to the surface.

medium.restatement: The induced surface charge explains why attraction works on neutrals: the unlike charge sits closer than the like charge, so attraction wins.
medium.analogy: A magnet near iron filings: the filings polarise and the nearest poles pull hardest.
medium.examPointer: For the acetate-cloth pair, name both directions: electrons rod-to-cloth, so rod positive and cloth negative.

check.stem: Before any friction, everyday objects are:

options.explanation: Charge is evenly spread — equal positives and negatives.
Nothing has moved the electrons yet.
Same — no transfer has occurred.
Sparking needs a large built-up charge.

check.stem: During friction charging, the object receiving electrons becomes:

options.explanation: Receiving negatives tips the balance negative.
The balance has tipped.
It has gained charge, not lost it.
Extra electrons make the receiver negative.

check.stem: A charged rod attracts a neutral object because:

options.explanation: Nothing doubles on approach.

options.text: opposite charge gathers on the neutral object's surface
options.explanation: The induced surface charge sits nearer the rod, so attraction wins.
Protons never move.
Gravity is irrelevant here.

check.stem: When an acetate rod is rubbed with a cloth, electrons move:

options.explanation: That would charge the rod negative.
The rubbing does transfer electrons.
The acetate loses electrons to the cloth.
Equal swapping would leave both neutral.

check.stem: After separation, the acetate rod and cloth:

options.explanation: Opposite charges on the two objects pull them together.
Repulsion needs like charges.
The charged pair exerts a force.
In air, with no path, the charges persist.

check.stem: Describe the charge state of the rod and the cloth after an acetate rod is rubbed.
check.modelAnswer: The cloth gains electrons and is negative; the rod loses them and is positive.

check.stem: How does a charged object pull on a neutral one?
check.modelAnswer: It attracts the opposite charge towards the neutral object's surface, so unlike charges meet and attract.

check.stem: Explain why only electron movement can explain friction charging.
check.modelAnswer: Positive protons stay locked in nuclei, so any transfer between surfaces must be the mobile negative electrons; that alone flips one object negative and the other positive.

check.stem: A rubbed acetate rod hangs near its cloth and swings toward it. Explain fully, naming the charges.
check.modelAnswer: Rubbing moved electrons from rod to cloth, so the cloth is negative and the rod positive; the opposite charges attract once separated.

glossary.definition: Having equal positive and negative charge, adding to zero.
A force acting between objects that are not touching.
Producing electrostatic charge on two insulators by rubbing them together.
Opposite charge drawn to a neutral object's surface by a nearby charged object.
